results.title: Upcoming SaladCloud Price Changes: September 12, 2026 - SaladCloud Blog
highlights:
SaladCloud GPU and vCPU pricing is changing on September 12, 2026: 15 GPU classes drop 25% on average, while RTX 5090 and 4090 prices increase.

Jared Carpenter

Product Update SaladCloud Tue Sep 01 2026

We're updating GPU and vCPU pricing on SaladCloud to correct places where our prices had drifted out of line with demand: some classes were priced above what the market will bear, and a couple were priced below it.

These changes take effect Saturday, September 12, 2026 at 00:00 UTC, and they will impact active and running instances at that time.

## Summary Copy Anchor Link

- Prices for 15 GPU classes are coming down, by 25% on average at High Priority (individual classes fall between 16% and 38%).
- Lowest Priority pricing is staying stable, with the exception of the RTX 5080, where it comes down from $0.180 to $0.150.
- RTX 5090 and RTX 4090: we've had to raise High, Medium, and Low Priority prices on these two classes. At High Priority, the RTX 5090 moves from $0.450 to $0.500 and the RTX 4090 from $0.300 to $0.330.
- For CPU-only workloads, vCPU pricing is going up from $0.004 to $0.005 per vCPU per hour. RAM pricing is unchanged. GPU container groups aren't charged for vCPU or RAM.
- Every GPU class not listed below is unchanged.

results.title: Fireworks raises GPU rates up to 30% • The Weighted Average
highlights:
Follows up on Owning a Model Costs $124K per Benchmark Point 

Earlier analysis of Fireworks’ Training API argued that a narrow team should train its own model only when specialization pays back roughly $124,000 per benchmark point plus engineering cost. Fireworks’ current on-demand price table raises H100/H200 from $7 to $8 per GPU-hour, B200 from $10 to $13, B300 from $12 to $15, and GB300 from $18 to $20 starting September 1—an 11%–30% increase. The call holds: dedicated reinforcement training still belongs to a narrow buyer set, but new runs should use the higher rates because Fireworks prices reinforcement fine-tuning by GPU-hour.

results.title: Nebius, Oracle, and Vessl AI Push AI Rental Rates Higher as Delivery Tightens | Drip
highlights:
AI rental prices are climbing as cloud providers monetize the growing cost and scarcity of delivering usable GPU capacity.

Updated September 28, 2026

## What is this trend?

GPU rental rates are rising as cloud and AI operators pass through higher costs for power, cooling, and delivery constraints on already-contracted capacity.

- • Nebius, Oracle, and Vessl AI are raising prices on specific GPU offerings, not the whole market.
- • Scarcity is shifting from chips alone to deliverable capacity: power, cooling, and site readiness.
- • Utility delays and high-density racks are making retrofits and interconnects a billable constraint.
- • Operators with power and thermal control can command higher rents and better margins.
- • Pricing is fragmenting by region and SKU as guaranteed access becomes more valuable than headline supply.

## What’s the latest?

September 28, 2026

Nebius raised selected Nvidia GPU rates 17%–21%, Oracle renewed expiring GPU contracts about 20% higher, and Vessl AI lifted H100 pricing in Korea by 24.7%, where local H100 rentals were up 21.9% month over month to $3.2

results.title: Cloud GPU Costs in India: Why 20% Is a Forecast
highlights:
Cloud GPU prices in India could rise 15–20% over the next 12–18 months, according to a forecast from Indian provider CloudPe, as expensive accelerators, memory, networking and power lift the cost of AI infrastructure. It is a provider estimate—not an announced industry-wide price increase—and ordinary storage or CPU cloud services are not automatically affected.

...

- CloudPe expects blended GPU cloud pricing in India to rise 15–20% over 12–18 months unless memory supply improves or alternative chips gain traction.
- The estimate applies to GPU-heavy AI compute, not every Indian cloud bill.
- Existing fleets and long purchase commitments can delay or soften price increases, while new capacity reflects current hardware costs faster.
- IndiaAI’s public calculator shows wide price differences by accelerator and commitment term, so buyers should compare workload cost rather than one headline hourly rate.
- Startups can limit exposure through smaller models, higher utilisation, reserved capacity and testing AMD, Intel or TPU alternatives where software allows.

A report published on August 31, 2026 has put a striking number on India’s AI infrastructure squeeze: cloud GPU rental prices may rise by 15–20%. The estimate came from CloudPe founder and chief executive Ishan Talathi, who linked the pressure to Nvidia hardware pricing and tight memory supply.

The story is fresh and relevant to India’s AI and technology sector, but the original draft overstated it as a broad rise in “Indian cloud costs.” CloudPe did not announce that all providers had raised prices, and the forecast does not apply equally to web hosting, databases, storage, CPUs and conventional business software.

...

CloudPe told The New Indian Express that, blended across its fleet and volume-purchase commitments, it anticipates Indian GPU cloud pricing to increase 15–20% over the next 12–18 months. Talathi attached two important conditions: prices could rise less if memory supply eases or alternative computing architectures gain traction.

The company also said it had acquired a significant share of its capacity before the latest surge. That can protect current customers in the short term because a provider prices rented compute from a mixed fleet bought at different dates and costs. A new data-centre expansion, however, must absorb today’s accelerator, memory, cooling and financing costs.

The forecast therefore describes a direction and range, not a fixed tariff. CloudPe’s public GPU pages currently advertise Indian instances from ₹36 an hour, while a documented H200 configuration is listed around ₹300 an hour. Those figures describe different machines and service configurations; they should not be compared as if every “GPU hour” were identical.

...

IndiaAI’s official compute portal provides a useful reality check because it lists accelerator options and prices from empanelled providers. The public calculator shows that an hourly rate changes sharply by chip, memory, instance size and commitment period.

At the time checked, the portal listed examples including an Intel Gaudi 2 configuration at ₹57.60 on demand, an AMD MI300X single-GPU instance around ₹168.20, and a two-GPU Nvidia B200 configuration around ₹581.40. A two-GPU Nvidia H200 NVL entry appeared around ₹292.75 per hour on demand. These are catalogue snapshots, not a universal market average, and included CPU, RAM or storage configurations may differ.

| Illustrative IndiaAI listing | Accelerators | On-demand rate | Why comparison is difficult |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Intel Gaudi 2.1x | 1 | ₹57.60/hour | Different software ecosystem and performance profile |
| AMD MI300X.1x | 1 | ₹168.20/hour | 256 GB memory; workload compatibility matters |
| Nvidia H200 NVL.2x | 2 | ₹292.75/hour | Two accelerators and 282 GB total GPU memory |
| Nvidia B200 SXM.2x | 2 | ₹581.40/hour | Newer Blackwell system with different throughput |

...

Commitment discounts can help predictable workloads. CloudPe’s own documentation shows monthly and longer billing periods with discounts that can reach 20% for an annual commitment on one illustrated H200 configuration. The trade-off is lock-in: unused reserved capacity can cost more than flexible on-demand access.

...

The accurate takeaway is narrow but important: one Indian provider expects cloud GPU prices to rise 15–20% over 12–18 months, not all cloud services to jump immediately. The impact will depend on each provider’s fleet cost, each customer’s contract and how efficiently the workload uses expensive accelerators.

results.title: You are negotiating the wrong term for your AI contract — Aureak
highlights:
In September 2026 an identical H100 rented for anywhere between $1.49 and $10.98 an hour, and spot prices were up a third on the year for a three-year-old chip. No rate you negotiate survives that, while the terms that decide the outcome are signed without much negotiation.

...

Start with a fact that ought to be impossible in a functioning market. In September 2026, renting one H100 for one hour cost between $1.49 and $10.98 depending on where you bought it — Vast.ai’s peer-to-peer floor at the bottom, Google Cloud’s a3-highgpu-8g list price at the top, for the same silicon. 1 Cross-provider medians land in between and disagree with each other: AIMultiple tracked $3.38 in August 2026, the Mercatus index $3.84 across 27 providers in September. 2 

Now the direction. The expected pattern for a three-year-old chip is steady decline as newer silicon takes the premium workloads. That is not what happened. Bank of America put H100 spot at $2.77–$2.80 an hour in August 2026 — up 2% on the month and up 33% on the year. A100 pricing, on a chip two generations old, was up 17% year on year. 2 

Anyone who signed a multi-year fixed-rate commitment in 2024, when H100 rentals were above $7 an hour, is now paying well above the market median. Anyone who deliberately stayed on spot through 2026 expecting further declines paid a third more than they budgeted. Both bets were reasonable when made, and both are wrong in hindsight.

The reason is that the binding constraint moved, and it did not move to where anyone was looking. It is no longer GPU die output. Morgan Stanley described DRAM as having become the principal bottleneck in the AI buildout, with memory prices up roughly six-fold over the prior year as manufacturers redirected HBM and DRAM toward data-center parts. 3 Nvidia has been unusually plain about the consequence: CFO Colette Kress told analysts in November 2025 that “the clouds are sold out,” and by August 2026 Jensen Huang was telling investors the company had “supply for 70% growth, but demand is much higher.” Kress added that supply would remain a bottleneck at least through the end of fiscal 2028.

...

The same tightness shows up in captive silicon, and the buyers are saying so on the record. In April 2026 Anthropic committed more than $100bn to AWS over ten years and secured up to 5 GW of capacity spanning Trainium2 through Trainium4, with an option on later generations. Andy Jassy’s stated reason: the silicon is “in such hot demand.” 4 Hyperscaler list prices, meanwhile, move slowest of all, because they are set through multi-year commercial agreements rather than marketplace clearing: AWS cut P5 pricing 44% in June 2025, and the resulting $6.88 an hour is still roughly 2.7 times a marketplace rate. 5 

So the honest summary is not “prices fell.” It is that the same chip traded across a seven-fold range in a single month, moved in opposite directions depending on which tier you bought, and did so because of a constraint — memory — that was not the one the market had been watching. You cannot win this negotiation on price. What you can do is decide in advance what happens when the price you agreed turns out to be wrong. That is a question about terms.

...

results.title: The four public GPU floors we track held again this week: H100 $3.85, H200 $4.29, B200 $6.69, A100 $2.30, the lowest reviewed public on-demand rate per family (August 30, 2026). Underneath them … | Bobby Clay
highlights:
The four public GPU floors we track held again this week: H100 $3.85, H200 $4.29, B200 $6.69, A100 $2.30, the lowest reviewed public on-demand rate per family (August 30, 2026). Underneath them the transaction-based OCPI kept moving, on all four families, with the B200 index down 8.9% (Ornn x ICE, August 30). A held floor beside a falling index is a point-in-time gap, not a price cut.

The real motion was in the map, not the price. AWS listed its eight-GPU B300 (p6-b300.48xlarge) in two more public catalog markets this week, Hyderabad and Sao Paulo, bringing it to five AWS regions in our reviewed catalog. Across the clouds we track, publicly listed on-demand B300 now spans from about $7.85 (Nebius) to about $35.62 (AWS) per GPU-hour (August 30, 2026), up from about $7.85 to $26.15 a week ago as AWS added Sao Paulo. A catalog listing is not proof the instance is orderable, but the map is filling in faster than the price is settling.
